children.name: SKOverlay.AppConfiguration(appIdentifier:position:)
children.summary: Builds the overlay configuration that promotes a specific App Store app by its numeric identifier and picks where the banner sits.

children.name: SKOverlay.AppClipConfiguration(position:)
children.summary: From inside an App Clip, promotes the clip's parent app without having to restate its identifier.

children.name: SKOverlay.Position
children.summary: Chooses between hugging the bottom edge or floating raised to leave room for a tab bar or toolbar.

discussion: The configuration closure returns an SKOverlay.AppConfiguration naming the recommended app and the banner position. Its classic use is App Clips promoting their full app, but any app can cross-promote a companion title. The overlay is system UI, so installation and account handling never touch your process.
name: .appStoreOverlay()
summary: Shows an SKOverlay banner recommending another App Store app without leaving the current app.

discussion: It mirrors .chartOverlay() but renders beneath the marks, which suits shaded zones, watermarks, or images that data should draw over. The proxy lets you anchor background elements to data coordinates so they stay put across resizing and domain changes. Marks, grid lines, and axis content all composite above whatever you draw here.
name: .chartBackground()
summary: Draws custom content behind the chart's plot area, positioned via a ChartProxy.

children.code:
Chart(sales) { s in
    BarMark(x: .value("Month", s.month), y: .value("Amount", s.amount))
        .foregroundStyle(by: .value("Kind", s.kind))
}
.chartForegroundStyleScale([
    "Revenue": Color.green,
    "Cost": Color.red
])
children.name: .chartForegroundStyleScale(_:)
children.summary: Takes literal key-value pairs so each category name is tied directly to one shape style.

children.code:
.chartForegroundStyleScale(
    domain: ["North", "South", "West"],
    range: [Color.blue, Color.orange, Color.green]
)
children.name: .chartForegroundStyleScale(domain:range:)
children.summary: Supplies the category domain and a parallel array of styles, useful when categories come from data rather than literals.

children.name: .chartForegroundStyleScale(range:)
children.summary: Replaces the default palette with your own style list while letting the chart infer the category domain.

code:
.chartForegroundStyleScale([
    "North": Color.blue,
    "South": Color.orange
])
discussion: Passing key-value pairs pins each category to a chosen ShapeStyle, keeping series colors consistent across multiple charts and app themes. Domain and range overloads set the mapping indirectly when categories are dynamic. The legend automatically reflects whatever mapping you declare.
name: .chartForegroundStyleScale()
summary: Maps series values to explicit colors or styles instead of the automatic palette.

children.code:
Chart(sales) { s in
    BarMark(x: .value("Month", s.month), y: .value("Amount", s.amount))
        .foregroundStyle(by: .value("Region", s.region))
}
.chartLegend(.hidden)
children.name: .chartLegend(_:)
children.summary: Toggles the automatic legend on or off with a Visibility value.

children.code:
.chartLegend(position: .trailing,
             alignment: .top,
             spacing: 12)
children.name: .chartLegend(position:alignment:spacing:)
children.summary: Keeps the generated legend but moves it to a chosen edge with explicit alignment and gap.

children.name: .chartLegend(position:alignment:spacing:content:)
children.summary: Swaps the system swatch list for a custom view placed at the requested legend position.

code:
Chart(sales) { sale in
    BarMark(x: .value("Month", sale.month),
            y: .value("Revenue", sale.revenue))
    .foregroundStyle(by: .value("Region", sale.region))
}
.chartLegend(position: .bottom, alignment: .leading)
discussion: Legends appear automatically whenever a mark uses a by-value channel like .foregroundStyle(by:), and this modifier controls their placement and spacing or removes them with .hidden. A content-builder overload substitutes an entirely custom legend view when the swatch-plus-label default is not enough. Position options include top, bottom, leading, trailing, and overlay placements.
name: .chartLegend()
summary: Positions, restyles, or hides the legend a chart generates for its series.

discussion: This is where interactive behavior lives: an invisible hit-target view plus a gesture, converted through the proxy into data values, yields scrubbing, tooltips, and custom selection. Content is aligned to the plot area rather than the full chart frame, so axis regions are excluded from your coordinate math. For iOS 17 and later, the built-in .chartXSelection() covers the most common scrub case with far less code.
name: .chartOverlay()
summary: Layers custom views over the plot area with access to a ChartProxy for coordinate conversion.

code:
.chartPlotStyle { plotArea in
    plotArea
        .frame(height: 240)
        .background(.quaternary.opacity(0.3))
}
discussion: The builder receives the plot area as a plain view, so anything you can do to a view — frame it, background it, clip it — applies to just the region inside the axes. This is the sanctioned way to give the plot a fixed aspect ratio or height independent of labels and legends. Styling here does not affect axis label layout, which sizes itself around the result.
name: .chartPlotStyle()
summary: Applies view modifiers to the chart's plot area itself, such as fixed sizing, borders, or clipping.

code:
Chart(days) { d in
    BarMark(x: .value("Day", d.date, unit: .day),
            y: .value("Steps", d.steps))
}
.chartScrollableAxes(.horizontal)
.chartXVisibleDomain(length: 3600 * 24 * 7)
discussion: Combined with .chartXVisibleDomain(length:), it shows a fixed window of data — say one week of a year-long series — that the user drags through. Scroll position can be observed and controlled with the related chartScrollPosition modifiers, enabling jump-to-date controls. Axes stay pinned while the plot content scrolls beneath them.
name: .chartScrollableAxes()
summary: Makes a chart scrollable along the given axes so large datasets can be panned.

children.code:
Chart(entries) { e in
    BarMark(x: .value("Day", e.day), y: .value("Steps", e.steps))
}
.chartXAxis(.hidden)
children.name: .chartXAxis(_:)
children.summary: Hides or shows the whole horizontal axis with a Visibility value.

children.name: .chartXAxis(content:)
children.summary: Rebuilds the horizontal axis from AxisMarks declarations instead of the automatic ticks and labels.

code:
Chart(entries) { entry in
    BarMark(x: .value("Day", entry.day),
            y: .value("Steps", entry.steps))
}
.chartXAxis(.hidden)
discussion: Passing .hidden removes the default axis entirely, while the content-builder overload replaces it with your own AxisMarks configuration. Because the default axis is generated from the data's type and domain, you only reach for this when the automatic choice of ticks or label formats falls short. Everything from stride-based date marks to fully custom label views is expressible in the builder.
name: .chartXAxis()
summary: Customizes or hides the horizontal axis of a chart.

children.code:
Chart(prices) { p in
    LineMark(x: .value("Date", p.date), y: .value("Close", p.close))
}
.chartXScale(domain: startDate...endDate)
children.name: .chartXScale(domain:type:)
children.summary: Pins the horizontal domain to a range or category list, optionally changing the scale type at the same time.

children.code:
Chart(points) { pt in
    PointMark(x: .value("Day", pt.day), y: .value("Score", pt.score))
}
.chartXScale(range: .plotDimension(padding: 24))
children.name: .chartXScale(range:)
children.summary: Adjusts how the domain maps onto the plot width, typically to pad the first and last marks away from the edges.

children.code:
Chart(samples) { s in
    PointMark(x: .value("Frequency", s.hz), y: .value("Gain", s.db))
}
.chartXScale(type: .log)
children.name: .chartXScale(type:)
children.summary: Changes only the scale type, such as switching a numeric axis to logarithmic while keeping the inferred domain.

code:
Chart(prices) { p in
    LineMark(x: .value("Date", p.date),
             y: .value("Close", p.close))
}
.chartXScale(domain: startDate...endDate)
discussion: Pinning the domain keeps a chart's window stable while data streams in, and prevents autoscaling from exaggerating noise in small ranges. Overloads accept ranges for continuous data, arrays for categorical domains, and a ScaleType such as .log for logarithmic axes. The y counterpart .chartYScale() takes the same options.
name: .chartXScale()
summary: Overrides the horizontal scale's domain, range, or scale type instead of inferring them from data.

children.name: .chartXSelection(value:)
children.summary: Tracks a single x value under the user's finger, clearing back to nil when the gesture ends.

children.name: .chartXSelection(range:)
children.summary: Lets the user drag out a band along the x axis, writing the chosen closed range into the binding.

discussion: The binding is an optional of the axis value type, becoming nil when the finger lifts, so a RuleMark plus annotation conditioned on it produces the standard lollipop scrubber in a few lines. Range and y-axis variants exist for band selection and vertical charts. Before iOS 17 this required a hand-rolled .chartOverlay() gesture.
name: .chartXSelection()
summary: Adds built-in tap-and-drag selection along the x axis, writing the selected value into a binding.

children.code:
Chart(entries) { e in
    LineMark(x: .value("Day", e.day), y: .value("Steps", e.steps))
}
.chartYAxis(.hidden)
children.name: .chartYAxis(_:)
children.summary: Removes or restores the vertical axis wholesale using a Visibility value.

children.name: .chartYAxis(content:)
children.summary: Declares custom AxisMarks for the vertical axis, commonly to relocate labels to the leading edge.

discussion: It mirrors .chartXAxis(): a Visibility argument toggles the whole axis, and the builder overload swaps in custom AxisMarks. A frequent use is AxisMarks(position: .leading) to move value labels to the left edge, since Swift Charts defaults y labels to trailing. Multiple AxisMarks declarations can render marks on both sides at once.
name: .chartYAxis()
summary: Customizes or hides the vertical axis of a chart.

children.code:
Chart(samples) { s in
    LineMark(x: .value("Trial", s.trial), y: .value("Score", s.score))
}
.chartYScale(domain: 0...100)
children.name: .chartYScale(domain:type:)
children.summary: Locks the vertical domain to a given range so sibling charts share the same baseline and ceiling.

children.code:
Chart(entries) { e in
    BarMark(x: .value("Day", e.day), y: .value("Change", e.delta))
}
.chartYScale(domain: .automatic(includesZero: true, reversed: false))
children.name: AutomaticScaleDomain.automatic(includesZero:reversed:)
children.summary: Keeps data-driven bounds while forcing zero into view or flipping the axis direction.

children.code:
Chart(readings) { r in
    LineMark(x: .value("Time", r.time), y: .value("Delta", r.delta))
}
.chartYScale(type: .symmetricLog)
children.name: .chartYScale(type:)
children.summary: Switches the vertical scale type, such as to symmetric log for data that crosses zero across magnitudes.

code:
Chart(samples) { s in
    LineMark(x: .value("Trial", s.trial),
             y: .value("Score", s.score))
}
.chartYScale(domain: 0...100)
discussion: A fixed y domain is the difference between comparable small-multiple charts and misleading ones, since autoscaled axes exaggerate whichever series is flattest. Domain values outside the data are respected, so you can force zero into view for honest bar baselines. Scale types like .log and .symmetricLog handle data spanning orders of magnitude.
name: .chartYScale()
summary: Fixes the vertical scale's domain or changes its type, such as switching to a logarithmic axis.

code:
Text(person.name)
    .focusable()
    .copyable([person.name])
discussion: Introduced in macOS 13, this wires a focused view into the standard Edit menu so Command-C works without any NSPasteboard code. The payload closure is an autoclosure evaluated lazily at copy time, so you always hand over the current value. It pairs naturally with .cuttable() and .pasteDestination() to give a custom view full clipboard behavior.
name: .copyable()
summary: Registers Transferable items that the Copy menu command places on the pasteboard when the view has focus.

discussion: Unlike .copyable(), the action closure is expected to remove the data from your model before returning it, matching the semantics users expect from Command-X. The payload type is declared up front so SwiftUI can validate the command against the pasteboard system. Available on macOS 13 and later.
name: .cuttable()
summary: Handles the Cut menu command for a focused view by returning the Transferable items to move to the pasteboard.

children.code:
.manageSubscriptionsSheet(isPresented: $managing,
                          subscriptionGroupID: "21534970")
children.name: .manageSubscriptionsSheet(isPresented:subscriptionGroupID:)
children.summary: Variant that limits the sheet to one subscription group when an app sells several.

children.code:
Button("Manage Subscription") { managing = true }
    .manageSubscriptionsSheet(isPresented: $managing)
children.name: .manageSubscriptionsSheet(isPresented:)
children.summary: Presents the management sheet covering every subscription the signed-in account holds for this app.

discussion: Keeping cancellation and plan changes in-app is both better UX and encouraged by review guidelines for subscription apps. The sheet reflects the signed-in App Store account's subscriptions for your app, and dismissal returns the user exactly where they were. An iOS 17 overload scopes the sheet to a single subscription group.
name: .manageSubscriptionsSheet()
summary: Presents the App Store's subscription management sheet inside your app instead of bouncing to the App Store app.

children.code:
Map(position: $position)
    .mapControls { MapUserLocationButton() }
children.name: MapUserLocationButton
children.summary: A control that recenters the camera on the user and begins following their location.

children.code:
Map(position: $position)
    .mapControls { MapCompass() }
children.name: MapCompass
children.summary: The rotation compass that appears when the map heading deviates from north and resets it on tap.

children.code:
Map(position: $position)
    .mapControls { MapScaleView() }
children.name: MapScaleView
children.summary: A legend showing the current map scale, typically shown while zooming.

children.name: MapPitchToggle
children.summary: Flips the camera between a flat overhead view and a tilted 3D perspective.

discussion: The builder lists control views that MapKit positions in their platform-standard corners, replacing the default control set. Each control can be tuned with mapControlVisibility to always show, auto-hide, or stay hidden. For fully custom placement you can instead instantiate these controls anywhere in your own layout using a map scope namespace.
name: .mapControls()
summary: Declares which system map controls — compass, scale, location button, pitch toggle — overlay the map.

children.code:
Map {
    MapPolyline(coordinates: route).stroke(.blue, lineWidth: 5)
}
.mapStyle(.standard(elevation: .flat,
                    emphasis: .muted,
                    pointsOfInterest: .excludingAll,
                    showsTraffic: true))
children.name: MapStyle.standard(elevation:emphasis:pointsOfInterest:showsTraffic:)
children.summary: The default vector cartography with knobs for terrain, muted emphasis under overlays, POI filtering, and traffic.

children.code:
Map(position: $position)
    .mapStyle(.imagery(elevation: .realistic))
children.name: MapStyle.imagery(elevation:)
children.summary: Pure satellite imagery with no labels, optionally draped over 3D terrain.

children.code:
Map(position: $position)
    .mapStyle(.hybrid(elevation: .realistic,
                      pointsOfInterest: .including([.cafe, .park]),
                      showsTraffic: false))
children.name: MapStyle.hybrid(elevation:pointsOfInterest:showsTraffic:)
children.summary: Satellite imagery with roads and labels drawn on top, plus the same POI and traffic options as standard.

children.name: PointOfInterestCategories
children.summary: Filters which point-of-interest labels the basemap draws, from everything to an explicit allow or deny list.

discussion: Each style takes refinements — elevation: .realistic enables the 3D terrain and landmark treatment, pointsOfInterest filters which POI categories appear, and standard offers an emphasis option that mutes the basemap under data overlays. The style applies through the environment to the maps below the modifier. Imagery and hybrid styles change which map controls make sense, so revisit .mapControls() when switching.
name: .mapStyle()
summary: Selects the base cartography of a Map: standard, satellite imagery, or hybrid.

discussion: Offer codes let you distribute free or discounted subscription periods outside the App Store's standard pricing, and this sheet validates and redeems them without any custom entry UI. Redemption results surface through the completion closure, with the entitlement itself arriving via Transaction.updates. This is the modern SwiftUI replacement for the old SKPaymentQueue presentation call.
name: .offerCodeRedemption()
summary: Presents the system sheet for redeeming subscription offer codes.

children.name: .onDrag(_:preview:)
children.summary: Variant that supplies a SwiftUI view to use as the drag preview instead of a snapshot of the source.

children.name: .onDrag(_:)
children.summary: Starts a drag whose preview is a snapshot of the source view and whose payload is the returned item provider.

discussion: The closure runs when the drag begins and returns an NSItemProvider describing the data to move, which lets the destination be another app entirely. It predates the Transferable-based .draggable() modifier and remains useful when you need item-provider-level control such as file promises. An iOS 15 overload adds a custom preview view shown under the finger during the drag.
name: .onDrag()
summary: Marks a view as the source of a drag interaction by supplying an NSItemProvider payload.

children.code:
GridCell(item: item)
    .onDrop(of: [.image],
            delegate: ReorderDelegate(item: item, items: $items))
children.name: .onDrop(of:delegate:)
children.summary: Delegate-based variant that reports drag entry, movement, exit, and the drop point for reordering interfaces.

children.code:
Rectangle()
    .fill(isTargeted ? .blue.opacity(0.3) : .clear)
    .onDrop(of: [.fileURL], isTargeted: $isTargeted) { providers in
        importFiles(from: providers)
        return true
    }
children.name: .onDrop(of:isTargeted:perform:)
children.summary: Closure form that receives the dropped item providers and reports acceptance with a Bool.

children.name: .onDrop(of:isTargeted:perform:) with drop location
children.summary: Overload whose closure also gets the drop point in the view's coordinate space for placing content precisely.

children.name: DropDelegate
children.summary: The protocol behind the delegate overload, with performDrop required and validation and hover callbacks optional.

code:
Rectangle()
    .fill(isTargeted ? .blue.opacity(0.3) : .clear)
    .onDrop(of: [.fileURL], isTargeted: $isTargeted) { providers in
        handle(providers)
    }
discussion: The isTargeted binding flips to true while a compatible drag hovers over the view, which is the hook for highlight feedback. The perform closure receives NSItemProviders and returns a Bool indicating whether the drop was accepted; loading the actual data is asynchronous. For fine-grained control over entry, exit, and drop location, use the overload that takes a DropDelegate instead of closures.
name: .onDrop()
summary: Turns a view into a drop target for dragged content matching a set of uniform type identifiers.

discussion: The async closure receives the Product and a Result wrapping Product.PurchaseResult, so a successful flow still requires you to unwrap the verification result and finish the transaction. Attaching it high in the hierarchy centralizes entitlement processing for every ProductView, StoreView, and SubscriptionStoreView below. Related modifiers let you customize purchase options or take over the purchase action entirely.
name: .onInAppPurchaseCompletion()
summary: Observes the outcome of purchases started by StoreKit views beneath the modified view.

children.code:
Map(position: $position)
    .onMapCameraChange(frequency: .continuous) { context in
        heading = context.camera.heading
    }
children.name: .onMapCameraChange(frequency:_:)
children.summary: Runs a closure with an update context whenever the camera moves, at the chosen cadence.

children.code:
.onMapCameraChange(frequency: .onEnd) { context in
    let region = context.region
    let rect = context.rect
    let camera = context.camera
    reloadPins(in: region, zoomDistance: camera.distance)
}
children.name: MapCameraUpdateContext
children.summary: The value passed to the change handler, exposing the new camera, region, and visible map rect side by side.

children.code:
Map(position: $position)
    .onMapCameraChange(frequency: .onEnd) { context in
        fetchPlaces(in: context.region)
    }
children.name: MapCameraUpdateFrequency
children.summary: Selects between a stream of updates during gestures and a single callback once the camera settles.

code:
Map(position: $position)
    .onMapCameraChange(frequency: .onEnd) { context in
        visibleRegion = context.region
    }
discussion: The frequency parameter chooses between .continuous updates during gestures and .onEnd delivery once movement settles, the latter being right for triggering data fetches for the visible region. The context exposes region, camera, and rect so you can pick whichever representation your query layer wants. It complements the MapCameraPosition binding, which handles programmatic positioning rather than observation.
name: .onMapCameraChange()
summary: Reports map camera movement, delivering the new region, camera, and visible rect in a context value.

discussion: SwiftUI automatically enables or disables the Edit menu's Paste item based on whether the pasteboard currently holds the declared payload type. An optional validator closure can filter or transform incoming items before your action sees them. This completes the macOS 13 clipboard trio alongside .copyable() and .cuttable().
name: .pasteDestination()
summary: Accepts the Paste menu command on a focused view, delivering pasteboard contents decoded as a Transferable type.

code:
VideoScrubber()
    .persistentSystemOverlays(.hidden)
discussion: It takes a Visibility value and expresses a preference, not a command — the system can still show the overlays when it deems them necessary. Typical use is full-bleed media playback or immersive canvases where the Home indicator would distract. The setting applies to the whole hierarchy under the modified view.
name: .persistentSystemOverlays()
summary: Requests that persistent system UI such as the Home indicator be hidden while the view is shown.

children.code:
AlbumView()
    .photosPicker(isPresented: $picking,
                  selection: $items,
                  maxSelectionCount: 4,
                  matching: .any(of: [.images, .screenshots]))
children.name: .photosPicker(isPresented:selection:maxSelectionCount:matching:)
children.summary: Multi-selection variant with a cap on how many assets the user can pick.

children.code:
@State private var selection: PhotosPickerItem?

LibraryGrid()
    .photosPicker(isPresented: $showingPicker,
                  selection: $selection,
                  matching: .images,
                  preferredItemEncoding: .current)
children.name: .photosPicker(isPresented:selection:matching:preferredItemEncoding:)
children.summary: Single-selection form bound to an optional PhotosPickerItem, with an optional filter and encoding preference.

children.code:
@State private var items: [PhotosPickerItem] = []

AlbumView()
    .photosPicker(isPresented: $picking,
                  selection: $items,
                  maxSelectionCount: 4,
                  selectionBehavior: .ordered,
                  matching: .any(of: [.images, .screenshots]))
children.name: .photosPicker(isPresented:selection:maxSelectionCount:selectionBehavior:matching:preferredItemEncoding:)
children.summary: Multi-selection form bound to an array, with an optional cap and an ordered or default selection style.

children.name: PHPickerFilter.any(of:)
children.summary: Composes several filters so an asset matching any of them appears, alongside all(of:) and not(_:) for the other logic.

discussion: The picker runs out of process, so the app only ever receives what the user explicitly selects and needs no library permission for picking. Filters built from PHPickerFilter values such as .images or .screenshots constrain what appears, and a maxSelectionCount overload enables multi-select. Selections land in PhotosPickerItem values that you load asynchronously.
name: .photosPicker()
summary: Presents the system photo library picker from a boolean binding rather than an inline PhotosPicker button.

discussion: The popover appears only while the tip's rules and the app-wide TipKit configuration say it is eligible, so the modifier can stay attached permanently without spamming users. Dismissal, frequency control, and persistence are handled by TipKit's data store rather than your own state. Prefer it over a hand-rolled .popover() for feature education because eligibility is centralized.
name: .popoverTip()
summary: Anchors a TipKit tip to a control as a popover with an arrow pointing at it.

children.code:
StoreView(ids: tipIDs)
    .productViewStyle(.compact)
children.name: ProductViewStyle.compact
children.summary: A dense single-row treatment suited to lists where price and buy button share a line.

children.code:
ProductView(id: "com.example.pro")
    .productViewStyle(.regular)
children.name: ProductViewStyle.regular
children.summary: The balanced default that stacks the icon, name, description, and purchase control.

children.name: ProductViewStyle.large
children.summary: A hero-sized card that gives the product artwork and description room to sell a headline purchase.

code:
ProductView(id: "com.example.pro.lifetime")
    .productViewStyle(.large)
discussion: Built-in styles include .compact, .regular, and .large, trading density for prominence. The modifier flows through the environment, so applying it to a container restyles every ProductView and StoreView row inside. Custom styles are possible by conforming to the ProductViewStyle protocol and composing the provided configuration.
name: .productViewStyle()
summary: Chooses the layout treatment for StoreKit product views, from compact rows to large promotional cards.

children.code:
Button("Preview All") { selected = attachments.first }
    .quickLookPreview($selected, in: attachments)
children.name: .quickLookPreview(_:in:)
children.summary: Previews an item within a collection, enabling arrow navigation between all items.

children.name: .quickLookPreview(_:)
children.summary: Previews the single URL in the binding and nils it out when the user dismisses the viewer.

discussion: Setting the bound URL triggers the preview and the system clears it back to nil on dismissal, so presentation state stays in your model. It handles every format Quick Look supports — PDFs, images, video, USDZ models — with zero viewer code, and requires importing QuickLook. A collection overload previews a whole set of items with built-in next and previous navigation.
name: .quickLookPreview()
summary: Presents the system Quick Look preview UI for the file URL in a binding, dismissing when the binding returns to nil.

discussion: The sheet is the sanctioned way to let users report a problem with a purchase without leaving the app; Apple adjudicates the request, and your app learns the outcome through the completion handler and later transaction updates. You supply the numeric transaction ID from a verified StoreKit transaction. Offering it prominently can reduce chargebacks and support load.
name: .refundRequestSheet()
summary: Presents Apple's refund request flow for a specific transaction identifier.

children.code:
StoreView(ids: productIDs)
    .storeButton(.visible, for: .restorePurchases)
children.name: StoreButtonKind.restorePurchases
children.summary: Opts a store view into the Restore Purchases control, which is hidden by default.

children.code:
SubscriptionStoreView(groupID: groupID)
    .storeButton(.visible, for: .redeemCode)
children.name: StoreButtonKind.redeemCode
children.summary: Surfaces an offer-code redemption button inside the store view.

children.code:
SubscriptionStoreView(groupID: groupID)
    .storeButton(.visible, for: .policies)
    .subscriptionStorePolicyDestination(url: privacyURL, for: .privacyPolicy)
children.name: StoreButtonKind.policies
children.summary: Shows the terms of service and privacy policy links, which you can route with subscriptionStorePolicyDestination.

children.name: StoreButtonKind.cancellation
children.summary: Controls the close button a store view shows when presented modally, so you can hide it in a pushed screen.

code:
SubscriptionStoreView(groupID: groupID)
    .storeButton(.visible, for: .redeemCode)
    .storeButton(.hidden, for: .cancellation)
discussion: The first argument is a Visibility and the second a button kind, so the same modifier both opts into optional buttons and suppresses default ones such as the cancellation control. Several kinds exist, including .restorePurchases, .redeemCode, .policies, and .signIn. Apply it repeatedly to configure multiple button kinds on one store view.
name: .storeButton()
summary: Shows or hides auxiliary StoreKit buttons like Restore Purchases, Redeem Code, or policy links.

children.code:
SubscriptionStoreView(groupID: groupID)
    .subscriptionStoreControlStyle(.picker)
children.name: SubscriptionStoreControlStyle.picker
children.summary: Lists plans as selectable rows with one shared subscribe button beneath them.

children.code:
SubscriptionStoreView(groupID: groupID)
    .subscriptionStoreControlStyle(.prominentPicker)
children.name: SubscriptionStoreControlStyle.prominentPicker
children.summary: Like picker, but visually emphasizes the selected plan to steer attention toward a recommended tier.

children.code:
SubscriptionStoreView(groupID: groupID)
    .subscriptionStoreControlStyle(.buttons)
    .subscriptionStoreButtonLabel(.multiline)
children.name: SubscriptionStoreControlStyle.buttons
children.summary: Gives every plan its own purchase button, trading a selection step for one-tap checkout.

code:
SubscriptionStoreView(groupID: groupID)
    .subscriptionStoreControlStyle(.buttons)
discussion: The .prominentPicker style highlights the selected plan with a single subscribe button, .picker is a flatter variant, and .buttons gives each plan its own purchase button. Which style converts best depends on how many plans the group offers, so the modifier makes experimenting cheap. It only affects subscription store views beneath it in the hierarchy.
name: .subscriptionStoreControlStyle()
summary: Selects how SubscriptionStoreView presents its plan options, such as a picker or stacked buy buttons.

discussion: Small widgets are a single tap target, and this modifier defines the URL that arrives via .onOpenURL() when the user taps them. Medium and large widgets can instead embed multiple Link views, with .widgetURL() acting as the fallback for the remaining area. Only one widgetURL is honored per widget view hierarchy.
name: .widgetURL()
summary: Assigns the deep-link URL a widget or watch complication opens in the app when tapped.

children.name: Annotation(_:coordinate:anchor:content:)
children.summary: The common form: a title string, the coordinate, which point of your view sits on it, and the view itself.

children.name: Annotation(coordinate:anchor:content:label:)
children.summary: Takes a second view builder for the label, so the caption can be styled instead of being a plain string.

children.name: .annotationTitles(_:)
children.summary: Hides or shows the caption beneath annotations and markers without removing their glyphs.

discussion: Where Marker is fixed system chrome, Annotation renders any view hierarchy you give it — badges, avatars, live-updating gauges — pinned to the coordinate. The anchor parameter controls which point of your view sits on the coordinate, defaulting to center but often set to .bottom for pin-like shapes. Titles participate in the map's label layout engine to avoid collisions.
name: Annotation
summary: Places an arbitrary SwiftUI view at a map coordinate, with a label and configurable anchor.

children.code:
Chart(traffic) { t in
    AreaMark(x: .value("Hour", t.hour),
             y: .value("Requests", t.count),
             stacking: .normalized)
    .foregroundStyle(by: .value("Source", t.source))
}
children.name: AreaMark(x:y:stacking:)
children.summary: Fills from the baseline up to y, with a stacking method that decides how overlapping series pile up.

children.code:
Chart(forecast) { f in
    AreaMark(x: .value("Day", f.date),
             yStart: .value("Low", f.low),
             yEnd: .value("High", f.high))
    .opacity(0.3)
}
children.name: AreaMark(x:yStart:yEnd:)
children.summary: Draws a band between two y values per x, the shape behind confidence intervals and min-max envelopes.

children.code:
Chart(readings) { r in
    AreaMark(x: .value("Time", r.time),
             y: .value("Level", r.level),
             series: .value("Sensor", r.sensorID),
             stacking: .unstacked)
    .foregroundStyle(.teal.opacity(0.4))
}
children.name: AreaMark(x:y:series:stacking:)
children.summary: Adds an explicit series value so separate areas are produced without also coloring them by category.

children.code:
AreaMark(x: .value("Month", m.name),
         y: .value("Share", m.share),
         stacking: .center)
// .standard, .normalized, .center, .unstacked
children.name: MarkStackingMethod
children.summary: Chooses standard stacking, percent-normalized stacking, a centered streamgraph layout, or no stacking at all.

code:
Chart(prices) { p in
    AreaMark(
        x: .value("Date", p.date),
        y: .value("Close", p.close)
    )
    .foregroundStyle(.linearGradient(colors: [.teal, .clear],
                                     startPoint: .top,
                                     endPoint: .bottom))
}
discussion: By default the fill runs from zero up to y, and stacked areas emerge automatically when series share x values. Initializers taking yStart and yEnd instead draw bands, which is the standard technique for confidence intervals or min-max ranges. Gradient foreground styles fading to clear are a common treatment for a single-series area.
name: AreaMark
summary: A Swift Charts mark that fills the region between a baseline and the data values.

children.name: AxisGridLine
children.summary: Draws the grid line crossing the plot at an axis value, with optional stroke styling.

children.code:
AxisMarks { _ in
    AxisTick()
    AxisValueLabel()
}
children.name: AxisTick
children.summary: Draws the short tick outside the plot edge at an axis value.

children.name: AxisValueLabel
children.summary: Renders the text label for an axis value, accepting format styles for dates and numbers.

children.name: AxisMarks(preset:position:values:stroke:)
children.summary: Keeps the system-drawn grid lines, ticks, and labels but lets you pick their preset, edge, value set, and stroke.

discussion: The values parameter controls where marks land — automatic, explicit arrays, or strides like .stride(by: .month) for dates. Its content closure receives each resolved AxisValue, letting you mix AxisGridLine, AxisTick, and AxisValueLabel per position, even conditionally. A position parameter moves the whole axis, such as putting y labels on the leading edge.
name: AxisMarks
summary: Declares the grid lines, ticks, and labels for one chart axis inside a chartXAxis or chartYAxis builder.

children.code:
Chart(sales) { sale in
    BarMark(x: .value("Month", sale.month),
            y: .value("Units", sale.units),
            width: .ratio(0.6),
            stacking: .normalized)
    .foregroundStyle(by: .value("Region", sale.region))
}
children.name: BarMark(x:y:width:height:stacking:)
children.summary: The standard bar from a category and a magnitude, with optional explicit thickness and stacking control.

children.code:
Chart(shifts) { s in
    BarMark(x: .value("Day", s.day),
            yStart: .value("Start", s.start),
            yEnd: .value("End", s.end),
            width: .fixed(14))
}
children.name: BarMark(x:yStart:yEnd:width:)
children.summary: A floating bar spanning two y values, which produces range charts and simple Gantt-style timelines.

children.code:
Chart(tasks) { task in
    BarMark(xStart: .value("Begin", task.start),
            xEnd: .value("Finish", task.end),
            y: .value("Task", task.name),
            height: .inset(4))
}
children.name: BarMark(xStart:xEnd:y:height:)
children.summary: The horizontal counterpart: a bar from xStart to xEnd on a categorical y axis.

children.code:
BarMark(x: .value("Team", t.name),
        y: .value("Wins", t.wins),
        width: .fixed(24))
// .automatic, .fixed(24), .ratio(0.5), .inset(6)
children.name: MarkDimension
children.summary: Sizes a bar as an absolute point value, a ratio of its band, an inset from the band, or automatically.

code:
Chart(sales) { sale in
    BarMark(
        x: .value("Month", sale.month),
        y: .value("Revenue", sale.revenue)
    )
    .foregroundStyle(by: .value("Region", sale.region))
}
discussion: Bars stack automatically when multiple data points share a category, and .foregroundStyle(by:) splits them into colored series with a generated legend. Swapping which axis gets the categorical value flips between vertical and horizontal bar charts. Fixed-dimension initializers control bar width or height explicitly when the default banding is not what you want.
name: BarMark
summary: A Swift Charts mark that draws rectangular bars from plottable x and y values.

children.name: value(atX:as:)
children.summary: Converts a horizontal offset inside the plot into the matching data value of the type you request.

children.name: position(forX:)
children.summary: The reverse mapping: a data value on the x axis to its offset in the plot, for drawing custom markers.

children.name: value(at:as:)
children.summary: Resolves a CGPoint to a tuple of x and y data values in one call.

children.name: plotFrame
children.summary: An anchor for the plot area's rectangle, resolved through a GeometryReader to align overlays with the marks.

discussion: The proxy's value(atX:) and value(atY:) methods convert a gesture location into the nearest data-space value, while position(forX:) and position(forY:) go the other way for drawing custom markers. It is handed to the builders of .chartOverlay() and .chartBackground(), and also exposes the plot area's size and frame. This is the foundation of custom hit testing when the built-in selection modifiers are not enough.
name: ChartProxy
summary: Translates between chart data values and view coordinates inside chart overlay and background builders.

children.code:
Chart(prices) { p in
    LineMark(x: .value("Date", p.date),
             y: .value("Close", p.close))
}
children.name: LineMark(x:y:)
children.summary: One line through every point; multiple series need a by-value channel or the series variant.

children.code:
Chart(runs) { r in
    LineMark(x: .value("Km", r.km),
             y: .value("Pace", r.pace),
             series: .value("Run", r.id))
    .foregroundStyle(.gray.opacity(0.5))
}
children.name: LineMark(x:y:series:)
children.summary: Splits data into separate lines by a series value while leaving color and legend untouched.

children.name: .interpolationMethod(_:)
children.summary: Picks how points are joined: straight segments, smooth curves, or stepped lines.

children.code:
LineMark(x: .value("Day", d.day), y: .value("Forecast", d.value))
    .lineStyle(StrokeStyle(lineWidth: 2, dash: [6, 4]))
children.name: .lineStyle(_:)
children.summary: Applies a StrokeStyle so a line can be thickened, dashed, or given round caps.

code:
Chart(readings) { reading in
    LineMark(
        x: .value("Time", reading.date),
        y: .value("Temp", reading.celsius)
    )
    .interpolationMethod(.catmullRom)
}
discussion: Points sharing a series value are joined in x order, and .interpolationMethod() switches between linear segments, step lines, and smooth curves like Catmull-Rom. Multiple series can come either from separate LineMark groups or a single mark differentiated with .foregroundStyle(by:) or series:. Combining it with PointMark overlays symbols on the same data.
name: LineMark
summary: A Swift Charts mark that connects data points into a line, one line per series.

children.code:
LookAroundPreview(scene: $scene,
                  allowsNavigation: true,
                  showsRoadLabels: false,
                  badgePosition: .bottomTrailing)
    .frame(height: 200)
children.name: LookAroundPreview(scene:allowsNavigation:showsRoadLabels:pointsOfInterest:badgePosition:)
children.summary: Binds to an optional scene so the card updates whenever you swap in a new location, with knobs for labels and the badge corner.

children.name: LookAroundPreview(initialScene:allowsNavigation:showsRoadLabels:pointsOfInterest:badgePosition:)
children.summary: Takes a scene by value for one-shot displays where the location never changes after creation.

discussion: You obtain an MKLookAroundScene asynchronously from MKLookAroundSceneRequest — a nil result means no coverage at that spot — and hand it to the preview via a binding or initial value. The embedded card supports panning, and tapping expands into the immersive Look Around experience without extra code. Coverage is limited to regions where Apple has captured imagery.
name: LookAroundPreview
summary: Embeds an interactive Look Around street-level scene for a location, expandable to the full-screen viewer.

children.code:
position = .camera(
    MapCamera(centerCoordinate: peak,
              distance: 1200, heading: 90, pitch: 60)
)
children.name: MapCameraPosition.camera()
children.summary: Positions the camera explicitly with a MapCamera, including distance, heading, and pitch.

children.code: position = .userLocation(fallback: .automatic)
children.name: MapCameraPosition.userLocation()
children.summary: Follows the user's location, falling back to another position until it is available.

children.code:
position = .region(MKCoordinateRegion(
    center: coordinate,
    latitudinalMeters: 2000,
    longitudinalMeters: 2000))
children.name: MapCameraPosition.region(_:)
children.summary: Frames an MKCoordinateRegion, the simplest way to show a place with a given span.

children.code:
position = .camera(
    MapCamera(centerCoordinate: peak,
              distance: 1200,
              heading: 90,
              pitch: 60)
)
children.name: MapCameraPosition.camera(_:)
children.summary: Places the camera exactly with a MapCamera, including distance, heading, and pitch for 3D views.

code:
@State private var position: MapCameraPosition = .region(
    MKCoordinateRegion(
        center: sanFrancisco,
        span: MKCoordinateSpan(latitudeDelta: 0.05,
                               longitudeDelta: 0.05))
)

Map(position: $position)
discussion: Static constructors cover the useful cases: .region for a coordinate span, .camera for full control including pitch and heading via MapCamera, .item to frame an MKMapItem, .userLocation with a fallback, and .automatic to frame the map's content. Bound to Map(position:), it is two-way — user panning flips the value's positionedByUser flag and setting a new value animates the camera. Assigning .automatic again reframes whatever content the map currently shows.
name: MapCameraPosition
summary: Describes where a SwiftUI Map's camera should be, from explicit regions to follow-the-user modes.

children.code:
MapCircle(center: store.coordinate, radius: 250)
    .foregroundStyle(.blue.opacity(0.2))
    .stroke(.blue, lineWidth: 2)
children.name: MapCircle(center:radius:)
children.summary: Builds the overlay from a center coordinate and a radius in meters.

children.name: MapCircle(_:)
children.summary: Wraps an existing MKCircle, which is convenient when the geofence already lives in CoreLocation-era code.

children.code:
MapCircle(center: center, radius: 800)
    .foregroundStyle(.red.opacity(0.15))
    .mapOverlayLevel(level: .aboveLabels)
children.name: .mapOverlayLevel(level:)
children.summary: Decides whether the overlay draws beneath the map's labels or above everything.

discussion: Because the radius is specified in real-world meters, the drawn size tracks the camera's zoom, which suits geofence and coverage visualizations. Fill and stroke come from foregroundStyle and stroke modifiers, and .mapOverlayLevel(level:) chooses whether it draws above roads or above labels. It conforms to MapContent, so it composes freely with markers and other overlays.
name: MapCircle
summary: Renders a filled circle overlay of a given radius in meters around a center coordinate.

children.name: MapPolygon(coordinates:)
children.summary: Creates the polygon from an ordered list of coordinates, implicitly closing the last edge.

children.name: MapPolygon(points:)
children.summary: Accepts MKMapPoint values in projected map space, handy when vertices come from map-rect math.

children.name: MapPolygon(_:)
children.summary: Wraps an MKPolygon, so overlays decoded from GeoJSON or older MapKit code render without conversion.

discussion: The polygon closes itself between the last and first coordinates, and also initializes directly from an existing MKPolygon for interop with older MapKit code. Semi-transparent foreground styles are the usual choice so the base map remains readable underneath. Zone boundaries, districts, and property outlines are its typical jobs.
name: MapPolygon
summary: Fills an arbitrary polygonal region on the map defined by its vertex coordinates.

children.code:
MapPolyline(coordinates: [tokyo, sanFrancisco],
            contourStyle: .geodesic)
    .stroke(.orange, lineWidth: 3)
children.name: MapPolyline(coordinates:contourStyle:)
children.summary: Connects coordinates in order, with a contour style that can follow great-circle arcs instead of straight segments.

children.name: MapPolyline(_ route: MKRoute)
children.summary: Draws the polyline of a directions result directly, the one-liner for turn-by-turn overlays.

children.name: MapPolyline(_ polyline: MKPolyline)
children.summary: Wraps an existing MKPolyline such as a recorded GPS track.

children.code:
MapPolyline(coordinates: plannedRoute)
    .stroke(.gray, style: StrokeStyle(lineWidth: 4,
                                      lineCap: .round,
                                      dash: [8, 8]))
children.name: .stroke(_:style:)
children.summary: Strokes the overlay with a full StrokeStyle for dashes, caps, and joins rather than a bare width.

discussion: It accepts raw coordinate arrays, an MKPolyline, or the polyline off an MKRoute, making turn-by-turn route rendering a one-liner after a directions request. The .stroke modifier takes any ShapeStyle plus line width, and StrokeStyle overloads add dashes and caps. Geodesic contours are supported via the contourStyle initializer parameter.
name: MapPolyline
summary: Draws a stroked path over the map through a sequence of coordinates or an MKRoute.

children.name: MapProxy.convert(_ point:from:)
children.summary: Turns a point in the given coordinate space into a map coordinate, returning nil when it falls off the map.

children.name: MapProxy.convert(_ coordinate:to:)
children.summary: Projects a map coordinate into view space so custom SwiftUI content can be positioned over it.

children.name: MapProxy.convert(_ rect:from:)
children.summary: Converts a rectangle of the view into the coordinate region it covers, useful for area selections.

discussion: The proxy's convert(_:from:) methods translate a tap location into a CLLocationCoordinate2D and back, which is the missing piece for drop-a-pin interactions. It wraps the map the way GeometryReader wraps ordinary views, passing the proxy into its content closure. Conversions respect the current camera, so results stay correct mid-gesture.
name: MapReader
summary: Provides a MapProxy for converting between screen points and map coordinates around a Map.

children.name: Marker(item:)
children.summary: Creates a marker from an MKMapItem, adopting the place's name and category styling.

children.name: Marker(_:coordinate:)
children.summary: A titled balloon at a coordinate using the default pin glyph.

children.name: Marker(_:systemImage:coordinate:)
children.summary: Uses an SF Symbol as the balloon glyph.

children.name: Marker(_:monogram:coordinate:)
children.summary: Shows short text such as initials or a number inside the balloon instead of an icon.

discussion: Markers get the standard Apple Maps look with a title and an optional glyph — an SF Symbol, monogram, or image — and accept .tint for color. They conform to MapContent rather than View, living only inside a Map's content builder. Initializers also accept an MKMapItem, inheriting the place's name and point-of-interest styling.
name: Marker
summary: A system-styled balloon pin placed at a coordinate inside a SwiftUI Map's content builder.

children.name: makeNSViewController(context:)
children.summary: Builds the AppKit controller once; wire the coordinator in here so delegate traffic flows from the start.

children.name: updateNSViewController(_:context:)
children.summary: Pushes the latest SwiftUI state into the controller on every relevant redraw; keep it cheap and idempotent.

children.name: makeCoordinator()
children.summary: Creates the object that receives AppKit delegate callbacks and forwards them back into SwiftUI bindings.

children.name: sizeThatFits(_:nsViewController:context:)
children.summary: Lets the wrapper answer layout proposals itself instead of taking whatever size the parent offers.

discussion: The shape mirrors UIViewControllerRepresentable: makeNSViewController constructs the controller, updateNSViewController synchronizes it with current SwiftUI state, and an optional Coordinator receives AppKit delegate traffic. It is the standard escape hatch for AppKit-only functionality like NSTextView-based editors or PDFView wrappers. Keep expensive setup in make and treat update as idempotent.
name: NSViewControllerRepresentable
summary: Bridges an AppKit view controller into SwiftUI on macOS.

children.name: loadTransferable(type:)
children.summary: Asynchronously decodes the asset into the Transferable type you ask for, returning nil when it cannot.

children.name: loadTransferable(type:completionHandler:)
children.summary: The callback-based variant that also hands back a Progress object for showing load state.

children.name: supportedContentTypes
children.summary: The uniform types the asset can be delivered as, letting you branch before requesting a Live Photo or movie.

children.name: itemIdentifier
children.summary: The PHAsset local identifier, populated only when the picker was given a photo library, for later PhotoKit fetches.

discussion: The item deliberately withholds the asset data until you call loadTransferable(type:), which decodes into any compatible Transferable type such as Data or a custom movie wrapper. This keeps large originals out of memory until needed and preserves the picker's privacy model. The itemIdentifier is only populated when the picker was configured with photo library access.
name: PhotosPickerItem
summary: An opaque token for one asset the user chose in the photos picker, loaded on demand via Transferable.

children.name: PlottableValue.value(_:_:)
children.summary: The factory behind every .value call: a label for axes and accessibility paired with the plotted value.

children.name: Plottable.primitivePlottable
children.summary: Adopting Plottable means exposing a primitive stand-in (a number, string, or date) that the chart actually scales.

children.name: Plottable.init?(primitivePlottable:)
children.summary: The reverse mapping the chart uses when it needs to hand a domain value back, such as in selection bindings.

discussion: Every mark parameter written as .value("Label", someValue) is constructing a PlottableValue, and the label becomes the dimension's name in generated axis titles and VoiceOver output. The wrapped value must conform to Plottable, which numeric types, strings, and dates do out of the box. Custom types can adopt Plottable to plot domain models directly.
name: PlottableValue
summary: Pairs a data value with the label Swift Charts uses for axes, legends, and accessibility.

children.code:
Chart(specimens) { s in
    PointMark(x: .value("Height", s.height),
              y: .value("Weight", s.weight))
}
children.name: PointMark(x:y:)
children.summary: One symbol per data point at the given x and y.

children.name: .symbol(_:)
children.summary: Uses a fixed glyph shape for every point, chosen from the built-in symbol shapes.

children.code:
PointMark(x: .value("Height", s.height), y: .value("Weight", s.weight))
    .symbol(by: .value("Species", s.species))
children.name: .symbol(by:)
children.summary: Varies the glyph shape per category and adds that mapping to the legend.

children.code:
PointMark(x: .value("GDP", c.gdp), y: .value("Life", c.lifeExpectancy))
    .symbolSize(by: .value("Population", c.population))
children.name: .symbolSize(by:)
children.summary: Scales each symbol's area by a numeric value, turning a scatter plot into a bubble chart.

code:
Chart(specimens) { s in
    PointMark(
        x: .value("Height", s.height),
        y: .value("Weight", s.weight)
    )
    .symbol(by: .value("Species", s.species))
}
discussion: Beyond position, points can encode extra dimensions: .symbol(by:) varies the glyph per category, .symbolSize(by:) scales area by a value, and .foregroundStyle(by:) colors by series. Those channel modifiers make a two-axis scatter plot carry four or five variables legibly. It also layers well over LineMark to emphasize the underlying samples.
name: PointMark
summary: A Swift Charts mark that plots individual data points, the basis of scatter plots.

children.code:
Chart(cells) { cell in
    RectangleMark(x: .value("Hour", cell.hour),
                  y: .value("Day", cell.day),
                  width: .ratio(0.9),
                  height: .ratio(0.9))
    .foregroundStyle(by: .value("Load", cell.load))
}
children.name: RectangleMark(x:y:width:height:)
children.summary: A cell centered on categorical x and y values, sized by the axis bands unless you override the dimensions.

children.code:
RectangleMark(xStart: .value("From", window.lowerBound),
              xEnd: .value("To", window.upperBound),
              yStart: .value("Low", 0),
              yEnd: .value("High", 100))
    .foregroundStyle(.gray.opacity(0.15))
children.name: RectangleMark(xStart:xEnd:yStart:yEnd:)
children.summary: An arbitrary region bounded on both axes, for shaded windows and 2D histogram bins.

children.code:
Chart(candles) { c in
    RectangleMark(x: .value("Day", c.date, unit: .day),
                  yStart: .value("Open", c.open),
                  yEnd: .value("Close", c.close),
                  width: .ratio(0.6))
    .foregroundStyle(c.close >= c.open ? .green : .red)
}
children.name: RectangleMark(x:yStart:yEnd:width:)
children.summary: A vertical band at one x position spanning a y range, such as a candlestick body.

code:
Chart(bins) { bin in
    RectangleMark(
        xStart: .value("Start", bin.start),
        xEnd: .value("End", bin.end),
        yStart: .value("Low", bin.low),
        yEnd: .value("High", bin.high)
    )
}
discussion: With start and end values on both axes it shades arbitrary regions, which covers heatmap cells, highlighted time windows, and 2D histogram bins. Supplying categorical values for both axes instead produces a grid of cells sized by the axis bands. Pair it with a value-based .foregroundStyle(by:) to get a color scale across cells.
name: RectangleMark
summary: A Swift Charts mark filling a rectangular region defined by x and y ranges.

children.code:
RuleMark(y: .value("Average", average))
    .lineStyle(StrokeStyle(lineWidth: 1, dash: [4]))
    .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
children.name: RuleMark(y:)
children.summary: A horizontal line across the full plot width at one y value, the classic threshold or average line.

children.name: RuleMark(x:)
children.summary: A vertical line at one x value, usually paired with a selection binding to mark the scrubbed position.

children.code:
Chart(samples) { s in
    RuleMark(x: .value("Trial", s.trial),
             yStart: .value("Min", s.min),
             yEnd: .value("Max", s.max))
    PointMark(x: .value("Trial", s.trial), y: .value("Mean", s.mean))
}
children.name: RuleMark(x:yStart:yEnd:)
children.summary: Constrains a vertical rule to a segment between two y values, useful for error bars and range whiskers.

children.name: .annotation(position:alignment:spacing:content:)
children.summary: Attaches a view next to the mark at a chosen edge or overlay position, ideal for labeling a threshold rule.

discussion: Fixing only y produces a horizontal reference line spanning the plot width; fixing only x produces a vertical one, the usual companion to a selection gesture. Giving both a start and end constrains the rule to a segment, useful for range indicators. The .annotation(position:) modifier hangs labels off the rule.
name: RuleMark
summary: A Swift Charts mark drawing a horizontal or vertical line across the plot, ideal for thresholds and annotations.

children.code:
SectorMark(angle: .value("Users", share.count),
           innerRadius: .ratio(0.6),
           outerRadius: .ratio(1.0),
           angularInset: 1.5)
    .foregroundStyle(by: .value("Platform", share.platform))
children.name: SectorMark(angle:innerRadius:outerRadius:angularInset:)
children.summary: One slice per data point sized by the angle value, with radii for donut holes and an inset gap between slices.

children.code:
SectorMark(angle: .value("Share", item.share),
           innerRadius: .ratio(0.5),
           angularInset: 2)
    .cornerRadius(6)

children.summary: Rounds the corners of each slice, which reads well on donuts with an angular inset.

children.name: .chartAngleSelection(value:)
children.summary: The selection modifier matched to sector charts: it writes the angle-domain value under the touch into a binding.

code:
Chart(shares) { share in
    SectorMark(
        angle: .value("Users", share.count),
        innerRadius: .ratio(0.6),
        angularInset: 1.5
    )
    .foregroundStyle(by: .value("Platform", share.platform))
}
discussion: Each data point contributes a slice proportional to its angle value, with innerRadius turning a pie into a donut and angularInset adding separation between slices. It arrived in the 2023 Charts update, finally covering part-to-whole charts natively. Slices pick up series colors and legends through .foregroundStyle(by:) like any other mark.
name: SectorMark
summary: A Swift Charts mark that renders pie and donut slices from an angle value.

StoreView(ids: ["com.example.tip.small", "com.example.tip.large"],
          prefersPromotionalIcon: true)

        .resizable()
        .scaledToFit()

code:
StoreView(ids: [
    "com.example.tipjar.small",
    "com.example.tipjar.large"
])
discussion: You pass the product identifiers and StoreKit fetches metadata, localizes prices, and handles purchases without any custom transaction UI. It is the quickest path to a tip jar or a small catalog of non-consumables, while ProductView covers single-product placement and SubscriptionStoreView covers subscription groups. Purchase outcomes can be observed with .onInAppPurchaseCompletion().
name: StoreView

discussion: Given a subscription group ID, it loads the products, renders plan options with localized pricing and introductory offers, and runs the whole purchase flow. A trailing view builder supplies your marketing header, and companion modifiers control which auxiliary buttons and control styles appear. It also understands the subscriber's current status, showing upgrade and downgrade choices appropriately.
name: SubscriptionStoreView
summary: A complete StoreKit merchandising screen for an auto-renewable subscription group, including plan picking and purchase.

children.name: Tip.rules
children.summary: Declares the conditions, built with #Rule over parameters or events, that must all hold before the tip may show.

children.name: Tip.options
children.summary: Tunes display policy, such as capping how many times a tip appears or ignoring the app-wide frequency limit.

children.name: Tip.actions
children.summary: Adds buttons to the tip; the identifier comes back in the TipView or popoverTip action closure.

children.name: invalidate(reason:)
children.summary: Retires the tip permanently, typically once the user performs the action it was teaching.

discussion: A conforming struct supplies title, optional message and image, and can declare rules built on parameters and events so the tip shows only when it is relevant — for example after a feature was used three times. Nothing displays until the app calls Tips.configure() at launch, which sets up the persistent store tracking impressions and dismissals. Calling invalidate(reason:) retires a tip once the user performs the action it teaches.
name: Tip
summary: Defines a piece of feature education: its content plus the rules and options governing when it may appear.

discussion: The view renders the tip's title, message, image, and any actions using the system tip appearance, and disappears automatically once the tip is invalidated or its display rules stop matching. An arrowEdge parameter draws a pointer toward the feature being taught. Inline placement suits tips about content regions, while .popoverTip() suits specific controls.
name: TipView

children.name: makeUIViewController(context:)
children.summary: Creates the UIKit controller a single time; this is where delegates are pointed at the coordinator.

children.name: updateUIViewController(_:context:)
children.summary: Called on every relevant SwiftUI update to sync the controller with the current state.

children.name: makeCoordinator()
children.summary: Produces the delegate or data-source object that lives alongside the controller and reports back to SwiftUI.

children.name: sizeThatFits(_:uiViewController:context:)
children.summary: Answers SwiftUI's size proposal from the wrapper so the controller can report its intrinsic dimensions.

discussion: You implement makeUIViewController to create the controller once and updateUIViewController to push SwiftUI state changes into it on every relevant update. A Coordinator object bridges delegate callbacks back into SwiftUI, typically holding bindings or closures. SwiftUI manages the controller's lifecycle, containment, and sizing within the surrounding layout.
name: UIViewControllerRepresentable
summary: Wraps a UIKit view controller so it can participate in a SwiftUI view hierarchy.

children.name: UserAnnotation()
children.summary: Shows the standard pulsing blue puck at the user's location.

children.name: UserAnnotation(anchor:content:)
children.summary: Replaces the puck with a custom view that receives the live UserLocation, including heading when available.

discussion: Adding it to the map content is what opts a SwiftUI Map into rendering the location puck; location authorization must already be granted through CoreLocation. A content-builder initializer swaps the default puck for a custom view that receives the current UserLocation. It pairs with MapUserLocationButton and the .userLocation camera position for follow-me behavior.
name: UserAnnotation
summary: Shows the user's live location on the map with the system's pulsing indicator.
